Bloomberg July 18, 2026 / 15:47 IST The production line for the C-Class sedan in a newly-opened extension to the Mercedes-Benz Group AG plant in Kecskemet, Hungary. (Image: Bloomberg) Hungary’s $20 billion electric-vehicle industry, which has long enjoyed the protection of former premier Viktor Orban, is facing a reckoning as the country’s new leadership cracks down on environmental violations and looks to raise taxes. The government plans to introduce the strictest environmental rules in the European Union, hiking levies on polluters and ending lavish tax breaks for multinational companies, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said late Friday. The steps are part of a broad overhaul to rebalance corporate taxation, he said. That’s putting businesses from China in particular on notice, a country that’s bet big on Hungary as a springboard to the EU market and which has set up some of the biggest battery plants there, as well as EV leader BYD Co.’s first factory in the bloc. They’ve been among the biggest beneficiaries of Hungarian subsidies. Magyar’s landslide election win in April was powered partly by a grassroots backlash against battery factories and concerns about land, air and water pollution after years of lax enforcement under Orban’s 16-year rule. One of Orban’s first moves after his return to power in 2010 was to scrap the environment ministry. “There is no compromise, there is no flexibility in terms of adhering to all the environmental rules,” Transportation Minister David Vitezy told Bloomberg in an interview. “This government won’t look away at any point just because of Chinese industrial interest if they don’t adhere to all Hungarian laws.” Related Stories China floods back into India's fertiliser market, offering cheaper supplies than UAE, Algeria, Egypt China's Wild Siberian tigers rise to 72 and Amur Leopards reach 115 after 10 years of conservation�... China backs India to hold ‘successful’ BRICS summit but remains evasive about Xi’s attendance The signs of change are visible. Last month, the government suspended the operation of Semcorp, a Chinese producer of lithium-ion battery separator films for the EV industry, after finding that the groundwater under the factory had been contaminated. Semcorp is located in the industrial park that rings the eastern city of Debrecen, a longtime Orban stronghold that’s slipped from his influence due to mounting anger over battery plants. Semcorp didn’t reply to a request for comment. Next door to Semcorp, Chinese battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. is finishing its $8.4 billion plant, the biggest single investment in Hungary’s history. It too is facing a probe over suspected polluting after a greenish liquid bubbled up around the plant in May. CATL, in a statement to Bloomberg, said water had been colored with a non-toxic as part of a storage tank leak test. CATL acknowledged its contractor had acted “improperly” by discharging it into the sewer system and said the company would be in “full compliance” with environmental regulations in the future. The action against Semcorp coincided with the launch of a police probe against BYD, which is suspected of illegally moving toxic soil from its construction site in the southern city of Szeged to an outside location. Environment Minister Laszlo Gajdos called it a “serious breach” of its environmental permit. BYD has denied wrongdoing. BYD this week signed Orban’s former foreign minister, Peter Szijjarto, as its new global head of external relations, a move that ruffled feathers with the Magyar administration. Szijjarto had been the point-person in bringing EV investments to Hungary and had channeled hundreds of millions of dollars in state subsidies to them, including to BYD. He’s also facing a probe over his ties to the Kremlin. “It’s now clear for everyone why he lobbied for Chinese car and battery makers, sacrificing Hungarian water and risking the health of Hungarians,” Magyar said on Wednesday. The newfound scrutiny is being noticed in China. One China-based adviser, who has organized investments tours to Hungary for Chinese businesses in the past, canceled a planned trip after Debrecen’s mayor called on polluting companies to leave Hungary. The person, who asked not be identified, said Chinese clients now saw heightened risks in investing in Hungary. That’s not the new government’s aim, said Vitezy, the transportation minister, who said the goal was to maintain Chinese ties while respecting local and European rules and regulations. Besides EV investments, Hungary is currently finishing work on the Belgrade-Budapest rail line that’s part of China’s global infrastructure Belt and Road Initiative. Since Vitezy took office in May, contractors led by state-owned China Railway Engineering Corporation have been retrofitting the line with European-standard signaling systems so that it can legally carry passengers in addition to freight. Vitezy praised the speed of the Chinese partners, saying it took them “half the time” it would’ve taken a European company to do, which he said raised questions about the competitiveness of European rail companies. When it comes to EVs, he said the government is aware that Chinese battery and car makers chose Hungary not only because of Orban’s backing but because of the country’s already robust vehicle industry. That eco-system in Hungary includes BMW AG, Mercedes-Benz AG and Volkswagen AG, as well as Suzuki Corp. which all have major factories in Hungary. Magyar this week inaugurated the expansion of Mercedes’s plant in the central city of Kecskemet, which company Chief Executive Officer Ola Kaellenius called a “benchmark in Europe.” “The fact is we have a strong economic alliance between China and the Hungarian economy, given its reliance on the car industry generally,” Vitezy said. “Many of those Chinese batteries are going into German cars.” Bloomberg first published: Jul 18, 2026 03:47 pm Discover the latest Business News , Sensex , and Nifty updates. Beállítom Donald Trump arról posztolt a Truth Socialön, hogy Ukrajna és Oroszország kölcsönösen beleegyezett abba, hogy nem támadnak energetikai célpontokat. Az amerikai elnök annyit tett még ehhez hozzá, hogy a dízel világpiaci árának emelkedését elsősorban az orosz–ukrán háború okozza, nem pedig Irán. Vasárnap arról beszélt a sajtónak Trump, hogy megkérte Zelenszkijt, ne lője az oroszok dízelt előállító infrastruktúráját , mert az az egész világnak árt. Az MTI szerint Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök azzal reagált erre a Telegramon, hogy Ukrajna kész leállítani az oroszországi energetikai létesítmények elleni támadásokat, ha Oroszország nem támadja az ukrán energetikai létesítményeket, a kritikus infrastruktúrát és az élelmiszerszállítást. "Ukrajna azt javasolta partnereinek, hogy segítsenek olyan megállapodást elérni Oroszországgal, amely megakadályozza a létfontosságú infrastruktúra megsemmisítését" – közölte az ukrán elnök. Zelenszkij nem biztos abban, hogy Oroszországnak szándékában áll betartani bármilyen megállapodást. "Ha a partnerek készek biztosítani, hogy Oroszország valóban ne támadja az áramellátásunkat, más energetikai létesítményeinket, a kritikus infrastruktúrát és az élelmiszerszállítást, akkor természetesen mi is készek vagyunk arra, hogy ennek megfelelően mi se hajtsunk végre támadásokat. Az ukrán elnök szerint az első lépés lehet a béke felé a létfontosságú infrastruktúrát érintő feszültségcsökkentés, de konkrétumokat vár az ügyben. Az elmúlt hónapokban Ukrajna több nagy hatótávolságú dróntámadást is indított orosz olajfinomítók ellen. A támadások csökkentették Oroszország üzemanyag-termelését, és az ország több részén is üzemanyag-hiányhoz vezettek. Kormányzati előrejelzések szerint Oroszország a háború hatásai miatt az idei üzemanyagtermelési várakozásait 17 éve nem látott szintre csökkentette, miközben a 2026-és és 2027-es évre vonatkozó üzemanyag-export előrejelzésein is változtatott. Ukrajna úgy látja, hogy az olajfinomítók legitim katonai célpontok, és az oroszok is támadják az ukrán energetikai infrastruktúrát.
